title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
lead: The Dead Sea Scrolls are the manuscripts found from 1947 on in eleven caves near Qumran, by the Dead Sea, and at other desert sites nearby. They include copies of books of the Hebrew Bible, copies of books outside it such as 1 Enoch and Jubilees, and the writings of a Jewish movement of the last centuries before Christ.

sections.b: The first scrolls were found in 1947 by a young Bedouin shepherd in what was later called Cave 1. Of the eleven Qumran caves with written remains, five were found by Bedouin and six by archaeologists. Cave 4 held thousands of fragments from hundreds of manuscripts, about three quarters of all the material from the Qumran caves: books of the Bible and books outside it, commentaries, works on Jewish law, prayers and the movement's own rules (Israel Antiquities Authority).

Hebrew fragments of Jubilees were found in at least five caves, Caves 1, 2, 3, 4 and 11 (Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library), and the Cave 4 copies were published by James VanderKam and J. T. Milik in 1994. The Damascus Document, a rule book of the same movement, refers its readers to "the Book of Time Divisions by Jubilees and Weeks" (CD 16:2–4). VanderKam (1992) counted fragments of twelve manuscripts; Matthew Monger (2014) argues that "there were likely not 14 complete manuscripts of Jubilees at Qumran." Devorah Dimant questions whether the Damascus Document really quotes the book. The scrolls' 364-day calendar, which Jubilees also teaches (Jubilees 6:32), is one reason the book is linked to this movement.
